analysis.one_liner: Requires members of Congress and their families to divest individual stocks or place them in blind trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in a Senate committee since its May 2025 introduction with no hearing or vote, backed by 19 Democratic senators and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force every member of Congress, plus their spouses and dependent children, to sell off individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives — or hand them to an independent-run blind trust — within months of the law passing, and bar them from acquiring new ones while in office. Diversified mutual funds, ETFs, and Treasury bonds would still be allowed. Members who don't comply would face a civil penalty equal to one month's pay, repeating every 30 days they stay out of compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who get a Congress whose members' personal finances no longer depend on picks of companies their committees oversee or laws affect. Members themselves also gain a clearer rule, but the main gain is public confidence in a body that currently lets lawmakers trade individual stocks that their own legislation can move.

how_it_helps.text: Every member, spouse, and dependent child must certify within 30 days and, within 120 days, divest or place each individual stock, commodity, future, or derivative — including through options or similar instruments — into an ethics-approved qualified blind trust.
Members would be barred from acquiring any new covered investment while in office, and inherited stocks would have to be divested or blind-trusted within 120 days.
Members could not dissolve a blind trust or regain control of covered investments until 180 days after leaving office, closing the revolving-door window.
The trust agreements, asset schedules, extensions, and any penalties would be posted publicly on the supervising ethics offices' websites.
Noncompliance triggers a written notice and then a civil penalty equal to one month of the member's salary, repeated at least every 30 days until they comply.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families who hold individual stocks would have to sell them or lose control of them to an independent trustee, giving up the ability to pick their own investments while serving and for 180 days after leaving.

drawbacks.text: The recurring penalty is capped at one month's pay per 30-day period, which wealthy members with large portfolios could treat as a cost of doing business rather than a deterrent.

The bill still allows diversified mutual funds, ETFs, and Treasury holdings, so members keep broad market exposure and their wealth continues to grow; a blind trust hides which specific stocks they own, not how rich they are.

Enforcement depends entirely on the supervising ethics offices issuing rules and levying penalties against the very members the law polices, so its strength in practice depends on how aggressively those offices act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest in dollar terms: lawmakers give up the right to trade individual securities, which no one needs to hold, in exchange for removing a direct conflict between members' personal portfolios and the laws they write. The bill's honest weaknesses are its lenient penalty and its dependence on ethics offices to enforce it, but neither undermines the basic rule; the design is reasonable, not watered down.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote while the session continues.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Ossoff introduced the bill on May 22, 2025 with eight original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The bill's entire recorded history is introduction and referral; no committee action, floor action, or vote has occurred.
Nineteen senators, all Democrats, have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold individual stocks are better off so far: the bill has not advanced, so no divestiture requirement or blind-trust rule has come close to taking effect, and the trading ban remains optional rather than law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lawmakers who trade stocks, so far

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 19 are Democrats, with no Republican support.

against.name: John Thune
against.what_they_did: Has not brought a congressional stock-trading ban to the Senate floor, where the bill cannot advance without his scheduling.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, though no vote has occurred that would show a party split on the floor.

industries.industry: Members of Congress with individual stock holdings
industries.note: The bill would force these members and their families to divest or blind-trust individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives and to stop acquiring new ones while serving. Their personal financial interest in keeping that trading freedom runs directly against the transparency the bill would provide the public.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in committee with no scheduled action and no Republican cosponsors, and similar stock-trading ban proposals in recent Congresses have died in committee without a floor vote. Advancement would require the committee chair to schedule action and the Majority Leader to bring it to the floor; absent a shift in Republican support, the likeliest path is that it stalls and expires with the 119th Congress.
